hints: Start by looking only at the dark-stained material in cells P, Q and R. Ask yourself for each cell whether you can see separate threads, a neat line, or just a diffuse mass with a dark spot.

Remember how DNA packaging changes through the cycle - it condenses to become visible in early mitosis, lines up in the middle at one stage, and spreads out as euchromatin for most of interphase when the nucleolus is visible.
Link each appearance to its stage: scattered condensed threads means prophase, a single row across the middle means metaphase, and no separate chromosomes plus a clear nucleolus means interphase.
walkthrough:
Reading P as Early Mitosis**
In cell P the dark chromatin has already condensed enough to see as separate worm-like chromosomes. They are scattered randomly through the nuclear area and the nucleolus has disappeared. That random arrangement of newly visible chromosomes is the hallmark of prophase.

Reading Q as the Middle Line-Up**
In cell Q all the thick, dark chromosomes lie in a single neat row across the middle of the cell. That central line is the equator or metaphase plate. Chromosomes only line up like this at metaphase, ready for equal separation.

Reading R as the Working Gap**
In cell R you cannot pick out any separate chromosomes. The nucleus looks pale and diffuse with a very dark round nucleolus inside. That means DNA is spread out as euchromatin for transcription and replication, which is interphase, the longest part of the cell cycle.

Final answer: P - chromosomes visible / chromatin condensing but randomly arranged in nucleus; Q - chromosomes aligned at cell equator / metaphase plate; R - no chromosomes visible / nucleolus present / chromatin decondensed as euchromatin.

hints: Think back to what happens in S phase before mitosis. How many copies of each DNA molecule are present when the cell reaches metaphase?
Picture the classic X-shape. The two copies must be identical in length and thickness and stay attached at one pinched point in the middle or near the middle.
Recall the vocabulary for parts: the whole copy on one side has one name, the join in the middle has a second name, and the protective tip at the end has a third name.
To earn all labels, draw one clear label line to one arm for the chromatid, one to the constriction for the centromere, and one to the very end of an arm for the telomere.
walkthrough:
Building the Correct Shape**
By metaphase DNA replication is complete, so one chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids. Draw them as two equal thick rods side by side forming an X, pinched together at the centromere. They must be the same length - different lengths would look like two different chromosomes.

Placing the Three Labels**
Label one entire side rod as a chromatid. A chromatid is one of the two DNA copies, not the whole X. Label the narrow waist where they join as the centromere, where spindle fibres attach via kinetochores. Label the very tip of either arm as the telomere, the repetitive protective cap that prevents loss of genes.

Final answer: Draw one X-shaped chromosome made of two identical sister chromatids joined at a constricted centromere. Label one whole arm as chromatid, the join as centromere, and the end of an arm as telomere.

hints: Think about what small basic proteins DNA wraps around to coil up tightly into nucleosomes and then into chromosomes.
walkthrough:
Packaging DNA**
DNA is a long acidic molecule that would be far too long to fit in the nucleus on its own. It winds around small basic proteins called histones to form nucleosomes, like thread around bobbins. Eight histones make the core of each nucleosome, allowing supercoiling into chromatin and chromosomes.

hints: Follow the spindle through time. First it must catch chromosomes, then hold them in the middle, then move copies apart.
Focus on where fibres attach and what has to split before movement can happen - think centromere and sister chromatids in anaphase.
Think about how microtubules themselves change length to pull chromatids to poles and later push the poles further apart.
walkthrough:
Capture and Line-Up**
Spindle fibres, made of microtubules, grow from opposite poles in prophase and attach to the kinetochore at the centromere of each chromosome. By pulling from both sides they manoeuvre chromosomes onto the equator or metaphase plate. This ensures one chromatid faces each pole.

Split and Pull Apart**
In anaphase the centromere divides and sister chromatids separate. Spindle fibres then shorten as microtubules disassemble at the ends, which pulls the now separate daughter chromosomes toward opposite poles. That shortening is what provides the force for segregation.

Push Poles Apart**
In late anaphase and telophase other spindle microtubules elongate between the poles, pushing the poles and the two new sets of chromosomes further apart. This helps the cell divide its genetic material into two equal groups before cytokinesis.

Final answer: Spindle fibres attach to centromere / kinetochore of each chromosome and move chromosomes to equator / metaphase plate; centromeres divide and sister chromatids separate in anaphase; spindle fibres shorten by microtubule disassembly to pull chromatids / daughter chromosomes to opposite poles, then elongate to push poles apart.
